are §3, §11/§12 and the FX client, is untouched: a pure function of three values
is neither a port nor a substitution seam.

**Rejected — `common`, beside `Money` and `Currency`.** It is where the two
types it operates on live, but `common`'s stated job is the vocabulary *every*
slice shares, and only `transfers` converts. Putting it there would grow the
package everything depends on in order to serve one caller. `fx` already owns
the Exchange Rate, and the conversion is a function of one.

The new edge is `fx → common`, one way, and the ArchUnit cycle rule covers it.

**Deferred — an `ExchangeRate` type.** `destination` and `exchangeRate` travel
together and will travel together again when ticket 26 locks a rate onto a
Transfer, which is the shape of a type wanting to be born, and CONTEXT.md
already names the concept. It is not born here because ticket 25 defines what
the provider actually returns — whether a rate carries its pair, its timestamp
and its validity window — and inventing that shape one ticket early would fix it
against a guess rather than against the port. Ticket 25 or 26 should pull it up
once there is something real to model.

**Not added to `Money`.** Ticket 06 held its surface to four methods on the
grounds that a fifth should arrive with a real call site. This is that call
site, and it still does not belong there: the operation needs a rate, which
`common` has no concept of, so `Money.convertedTo(…)` would drag `BigDecimal`
rates into the type whose entire point is that money is not a decimal.

## A rate of zero was a `422` blaming the wrong party

**Beyond what the ticket asked for, and caused by the shape it asked for.** With
round-to-zero as a reported outcome, a rate of `0` — a provider bug, or an
unparsed field defaulting — produces `RoundsToZero`, which ticket 26 turns into
a `422` telling the operator their transfer was too small. That answer is
confidently wrong about whose fault it is, and nothing downstream could tell.

`convert` therefore refuses a rate at or below zero with
`IllegalArgumentException`, the same way `Money` refuses mixed currencies: a bad
rate is a bug above this function rather than something a user asked for, so it
is an unchecked exception and nothing catches it. Ticket 25 may well validate
at the port too; this is the backstop that keeps the `RoundsToZero` outcome
honest, and it is cheap enough to keep in both places.

## What the arithmetic needed, and did not

**One expression, both directions.** `BigDecimal.movePointRight` takes a
negative argument and moves the point left, so `destScale − srcScale` is applied
as written with no branch on which currency has more decimals.

**Overflow is refused, not wrapped**, via `longValueExact`, matching the
`addExact`/`subtractExact` choice ticket 06 made for the same reason: a wrapped
count of Minor Units is the one way this representation can hold a quantity that
is not the answer.
=== 34 ===
**The same `?raw` trick closes a gap in the ticket's fifth requirement.** "Sourced from
the generated types" was satisfied only by `Record<ProblemType, …>`, and `npm test` is
`vitest run` with no type-check in front of it — so a URN the backend had grown reached
a red build but a green test run. The test now reads `schema.gen.ts` itself and pins the
URN list against the module's table. It cannot go vacuous: a regex that stopped matching
yields an empty list against ten entries.

This is the second copy of ticket 33's source-assertion block. It is left duplicated
rather than extracted, because a shared helper needs a home and two callers do not
choose one; [ticket 35](../../.scratch/global-payment-service/issues/35-idempotency-key-module.md)
adds the third, and that is when it becomes a test helper rather than a pattern.

## What is not settled here

**The FX body claims no money was moved.** §15 fixes the Exchange Rate at request time
and §27 fails the request when the provider will not answer, so a Transfer that never
got one never reserved anything. That is true of the design as written and it is a claim
about code [ticket 25](../../.scratch/global-payment-service/issues/25-exchange-rate-client.md)
has not built yet. If the Exchange Rate call ever moves after the reservation, this
sentence becomes wrong in the most alarming direction, and it is named here so that
ticket knows it owns it.

**The copy has to hold for a query and for a mutation both**, because the function is
not told which. The `internal-error` body originally said the request had already been
attempted more than once — true of a query, which `retry.ts` gives three attempts, and
false of a `POST`, which gets one. It says nothing about attempts now.
=== 24 ===
because here the configuration is the thing that can drift and the observable effect is
already pinned by something else.

Measured rather than argued: registering `/mock/**` on the CORS source turns
`mapsNoCorsPolicyOntoTheProvider` red and leaves
`allowsNoCrossOriginAccessToTheProvider` green, which is the whole finding in one run.

## Rejected — quoting from a table of pairs

Six hand-written rates can disagree with each other: an `EUR/HUF` and a `USD/HUF`
that do not agree with the same table's `EUR/USD` produce a converted amount that
is off by a remainder, and the first place anyone would look is ticket 07's
rounding. `QuotedRates` holds one figure per currency against a pivot and divides,
so cross-rate consistency is a property of the shape rather than of the numbers
having been typed carefully.

## The latency is applied before the failure is decided

So a `503` is as slow as a `200`. A provider that answered its errors promptly
would let a client's read timeout and its retry budget be tuned independently,
which is not the situation an unreliable third party puts you in — and it would
leave ticket 25's timeout with only the success path to fire on.

## Observed — Spring Security warns about the bypass at startup

```
WARN o.s.s.c.a.web.builders.WebSecurity : You are asking Spring Security to ignore
PathPattern [/mock/**]. This is not recommended -- please use permitAll via
HttpSecurity#authorizeHttpRequests instead.
```

The advice is right for endpoints that are ours and wrong for this one, which is
ticket 04's rejected alternative read in the other direction: there,
`ignoring()` on `/api/**` was rejected *because* it forgoes the security response
headers. Here that is the point. The warning appears only under a profile whose
whole purpose is to pretend, so it is left to print rather than silenced.

## What went to the README instead

The README carries the profile, the two dials and what turning each of them does,
since that is what someone running the thing needs. It also carries the
consequence §28 names — that the application now calls itself over HTTP, which is
what makes `spring.threads.virtual.enabled` load-bearing rather than a nicety.

# 3. The "three public ports" — house style

`payments/package-info.java` and §30 name them: **§3 idempotency (`IdempotentExecution`), §11/§12 outbox (`EventPublisher`), and the FX client (`ExchangeRateProvider`)**.

**Crucial finding: none of the three interfaces exists in code yet. Yours is the first.** So there is no interface to copy verbatim — but the *pattern* is fully specified:

**`src/main/java/hu/bankmonitor/payments/fx/package-info.java` (verbatim, lines 1–14):**
```java
/**
 * Exchange rates for cross-currency transfers, and the conversion one is used for.
 *
 * <p>Exports a port — asking for the rate between two currencies — and
 * {@link hu.bankmonitor.payments.fx.CurrencyConversion}, the pure function that applies
 * one. The provider is unreliable by design, so the HTTP client behind that port — its
 * timeouts, its retries and its mapping of failures onto this application's errors — is
 * package-private and replaceable without any caller noticing.
 *
 * <p>The split is deliberate: the arithmetic is the part most likely to be wrong and the
 * part easiest to test, so it is kept clear of everything that makes the provider hard to
 * test. The conversion knows nothing about where a rate came from.
 */
package hu.bankmonitor.payments.fx;
```

**The idempotency precedent** (`idempotency/package-info.java:10-13`): the slice shipped the *storage* under the port and deliberately left the port itself to the first ticket with a caller. §30's amendment (00-initial-decisions.md:1134-1138) says the same. **Read against ticket 26, the analogue for you is: the port + client ship now, because ticket 26 is the caller and it is blocked on you.**

**The only port-shaped signature written down anywhere** is §3's (00-initial-decisions.md:92-96):
```java
public interface IdempotentExecution {
    <T> T executeOnce(String key, String payloadHash, Supplier<T> operation);
}
```

**Shape:** plain `extends RuntimeException`, one per refusal, named `<Thing><Verb>Exception`, carrying **the facts** (not the status code, not the URN), with Javadoc that says *why it carries them* and explicitly defers the status to the endpoint ticket. Visibility follows the boundary: `public` when another slice raises/catches it (`accounts/InsufficientFundsException`, `accounts/UnknownAccountException`), package-private when it never leaves the slice (`transfers/CrossCurrencyTransferNotSupportedException`).

Verbatim, `accounts/UnknownAccountException.java`:
```java

 * Raised when a Transfer names an Account ID the table has no row for.
 *
 * <p>Carries the ID because the caller has two of them and the answer it owes the client
 * has to say which one was wrong. Whether that answer is a {@code 404} or a {@code 422},
 * and under which problem type URN, belongs to the endpoint in ticket 14.
 * …

public class UnknownAccountException extends RuntimeException {
	private final long accountId;
	public UnknownAccountException(long accountId) {
		super("no account with ID " + accountId);
		this.accountId = accountId;

# 5. Exception style + controller handlers

**Shape:** plain `extends RuntimeException`, one per refusal, named `<Thing><Verb>Exception`, carrying **the facts** (not the status code, not the URN), with Javadoc that says *why it carries them* and explicitly defers the status to the endpoint ticket. Visibility follows the boundary: `public` when another slice raises/catches it (`accounts/InsufficientFundsException`, `accounts/UnknownAccountException`), package-private when it never leaves the slice (`transfers/CrossCurrencyTransferNotSupportedException`).

Verbatim, `accounts/UnknownAccountException.java`:
```java
/**
 * Raised when a Transfer names an Account ID the table has no row for.
 *
 * <p>Carries the ID because the caller has two of them and the answer it owes the client
 * has to say which one was wrong. Whether that answer is a {@code 404} or a {@code 422},
 * and under which problem type URN, belongs to the endpoint in ticket 14.
 * …
 */
public class UnknownAccountException extends RuntimeException {
	private final long accountId;
	public UnknownAccountException(long accountId) {
		super("no account with ID " + accountId);
		this.accountId = accountId;
	}
	public long getAccountId() { return accountId; }
}

**`00-initial-decisions.md` — everything touching your ticket:**

**§27 "The flaky FX provider: timeouts, retry, then fail to the caller" (lines 925-963), verbatim:**
> No cache, no circuit breaker. Timeouts on the `RestClient`, `@Retryable` around the call, and on exhaustion a `503` with `urn:problem:fx-provider-unavailable` and a `Retry-After`.
>
> `@Retryable` is **built into Spring Framework 7**, so Boot 4 needs neither `spring-retry` nor Resilience4j. Two migration details that every tutorial predates: the enabling annotation is **`@EnableResilientMethods`** (not `@EnableRetry`), and `maxAttempts` was renamed **`maxRetries`**.
>
> - **Timeouts are non-negotiable.** Without them "responds slowly" is unbounded, and a virtual thread parks forever while holding an `IN_PROGRESS` idempotency claim — the flaky provider becomes a stuck transfer.
> - Retry `5xx` and timeouts. **Never retry `4xx`.**
>
> **Why the lean version is complete, rather than a corner cut:** §5 marks the idempotency record `FAILED`, which is explicitly retryable, so the client resubmits with the *same key* and the server executes properly. Failing to the caller is not giving up — it hands the retry to the layer that already has idempotency making it safe. §5, §15 and §21's retry policy cohere into one answer to the "handle the flaky API elegantly" requirement.
>
> **Rejected — a circuit breaker.** A breaker exists to protect a scarce thread pool from being consumed by calls that will fail. Virtual threads mean threads are not scarce, and the retry budget is already bounded by the timeout. Goes to [deferred.md](../deferred.md).
>
> **Rejected — caching rates.** A legitimate want, declined on scope. If it comes back: §15 already stores the fetch timestamp on the transfer, so a cached rate stays auditable.
>
> **Free win:** Spring Framework 7 publishes `MethodRetryEvent`, observable with `@EventListener`. A test can **assert that the retry actually happened** without mocking framework internals — resilience tested rather than claimed, on a graded line.
>
> Sources: `danvega.dev/blog/spring-boot-4-native-retry-support`; the `@Retryable` javadoc; the Moderne spring-retry → Framework 7 migration recipe.

# A. `@Retryable` / `@EnableResilientMethods`

## A1. FQCN — confirmed

`org.springframework.resilience.annotation.Retryable`, shipped in **spring-context** (`spring-context-7.0.9.jar`, entry `org/springframework/resilience/annotation/Retryable.class`). Declared `@Target({TYPE, METHOD}) @Retention(RUNTIME) @Documented @Reflective`, `@since 7.0`.

> ⚠️ **Import trap:** `org.springframework.core.retry.Retryable` also exists in spring-core and is **not** an annotation — it is the functional interface `Retryable<R>` that `RetryTemplate.execute(...)` takes. Both are on your classpath. `AbstractRetryInterceptor.java` imports the *core* one.

## A2. Every attribute, with types and defaults

`javap -p -classpath spring-context-7.0.9.jar org.springframework.resilience.annotation.Retryable`:

```
public interface org.springframework.resilience.annotation.Retryable extends java.lang.annotation.Annotation {
  public abstract java.lang.Class<? extends java.lang.Throwable>[] value();
  public abstract java.lang.Class<? extends java.lang.Throwable>[] includes();
  public abstract java.lang.Class<? extends java.lang.Throwable>[] excludes();
  public abstract java.lang.Class<? extends org.springframework.resilience.retry.MethodRetryPredicate> predicate();
  public abstract long maxRetries();
  public abstract java.lang.String maxRetriesString();
  public abstract long timeout();
  public abstract java.lang.String timeoutString();
  public abstract long delay();
  public abstract java.lang.String delayString();
  public abstract long jitter();
  public abstract java.lang.String jitterString();
  public abstract double multiplier();
  public abstract java.lang.String multiplierString();
  public abstract long maxDelay();
  public abstract java.lang.String maxDelayString();
  public abstract java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit timeUnit();
}
```

Defaults, from `Retryable.java` in the sources jar:

| attribute | type | default | notes (verbatim Javadoc points) |
|---|---|---|---|
| `value` | `Class<? extends Throwable>[]` | `{}` | `@AliasFor("includes")` |
| `includes` | `Class<? extends Throwable>[]` | `{}` | `@AliasFor("value")`; "matched against an exception thrown by a failed invocation **as well as nested causes**"; "The default is empty, leading to a retry attempt for any exception." |
| `excludes` | `Class<? extends Throwable>[]` | `{}` | same cause-traversal semantics |
| `predicate` | `Class<? extends MethodRetryPredicate>` | `MethodRetryPredicate.class` | "will be instantiated per method. It can use dependency injection at the constructor level" |
| `maxRetries` | `long` | `3` | "**total attempts = 1 initial attempt + maxRetries attempts**" |
| `maxRetriesString` | `String` | `""` | overrides `maxRetries`; `${...}` + SpEL |
| `timeout` | `long` | `0` (no timeout) | `@since 7.0.2`; wall-clock budget over initial + retries + delays |
| `timeoutString` | `String` | `""` | `@since 7.0.2` |
| `delay` | `long` | `1000` | base delay, unit from `timeUnit` |
| `delayString` | `String` | `""` | plain int, ISO8601 (`PT2S`), or SIMPLE (`2s`); `${...}`/SpEL |
| `jitter` | `long` | `0` | `delay-jitter .. delay+jitter`, never below `delay` nor above `maxDelay` |
| `jitterString` | `String` | `""` | |
| `multiplier` | `double` | `1.0` | applied to previous delay *and* to jitter |
| `multiplierString` | `String` | `""` | |
| `maxDelay` | `long` | `Long.MAX_VALUE` | |
| `maxDelayString` | `String` | `""` | |
| `timeUnit` | `TimeUnit` | `TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS` | applies to `delay`, `jitter`, `maxDelay` (+ their `*String` forms as fallback unit); ignored for explicit `Duration` strings |

**Differs from Spring Retry tutorials:** the attribute is `maxRetries` (retries *after* the first call), **not** `maxAttempts`. `@Backoff` does not exist — `delay`/`multiplier`/`maxDelay`/`jitter` are flat attributes on `@Retryable`. There is no `retryFor`/`noRetryFor`/`label`/`stateful`/`listeners`/`recover`/`interceptor` attribute.

## A3. `@EnableResilientMethods`

`org.springframework.resilience.annotation.EnableResilientMethods` (spring-context). `@Target(TYPE) @Retention(RUNTIME) @Import(ResilientMethodsConfiguration.class)`.

```
public interface org.springframework.resilience.annotation.EnableResilientMethods extends java.lang.annotation.Annotation {
  public abstract boolean proxyTargetClass();   // default false
  public abstract int order();                  // default Ordered.LOWEST_PRECEDENCE - 1
}
```

**There is no `mode` attribute** (no AspectJ mode). Javadoc: "Enables Spring's core resilience features for method invocations: `@Retryable` as well as `@ConcurrencyLimit`." It imports `ResilientMethodsConfiguration`, which registers exactly two infrastructure beans:

```java
@Bean(name = "org.springframework.resilience.annotation.internalRetryAnnotationProcessor")
public RetryAnnotationBeanPostProcessor retryAdvisor() { ... }
@Bean(name = "org.springframework.resilience.annotation.internalConcurrencyLimitProcessor")
public ConcurrencyLimitBeanPostProcessor concurrencyLimitAdvisor() { ... }
```

**Boot 4.1.1 does NOT auto-configure this.** Verified: `spring-boot-autoconfigure-4.1.1.jar` contains no class matching `retry|resilien`, and its `AutoConfiguration.imports` has no matching entry. You must put `@EnableResilientMethods` on a `@Configuration` class yourself.

Note also `configureProxySupport` only ever calls `setProxyTargetClass(true)` when the attribute is `true` — it never calls `setProxyTargetClass(false)`. See A7 for why that matters.

## A4. `@Recover` equivalent — **NO. There is none.**

Verified negatively two ways: `unzip -l` over `spring-context-7.0.9.jar` and `spring-core-7.0.9.jar` filtered by `-i recover` returns **zero entries**; `grep -r "Recover"` across the extracted `org/springframework/resilience/**` and `org/springframework/core/retry/**` sources returns nothing. The complete `org.springframework.resilience` package is:

```
InvocationRejectedException
annotation/{ConcurrencyLimit, ConcurrencyLimitBeanPostProcessor, EnableResilientMethods,
            ResilientMethodsConfiguration, RetryAnnotationBeanPostProcessor, Retryable}
retry/{AbstractRetryInterceptor, MethodRetryEvent, MethodRetryPredicate,
       MethodRetrySpec, SimpleRetryInterceptor}
```

Fallback is your own `try/catch` around the proxied call.

## A5. **CRITICAL — what the caller sees on exhaustion: the last thrown exception, rethrown as-is.**

`org/springframework/resilience/retry/AbstractRetryInterceptor.java`, `invoke(...)`, lines 132–151 (verbatim):

```java
try {
    return retryTemplate.execute(new Retryable<@Nullable Object>() {
        @Override
        public @Nullable Object execute() throws Throwable {
            return (invocation instanceof ProxyMethodInvocation pmi ?
                    pmi.invocableClone().proceed() : invocation.proceed());
        }
        @Override
        public String getName() { return methodName; }
    });
}
catch (RetryException ex) {
    onEvent(new MethodRetryEvent(invocation, ex, true));
    if (logger.isDebugEnabled()) {
        logger.debug("Retryable operation '%s' failed".formatted(methodName), ex);
    }
    throw ex.getCause();          // <<<<<< unwrapped
}
```

And `RetryException`'s cause is definitionally the last exception — `core/retry/RetryTemplate.java` lines 194–200:

```java
// The RetryPolicy has exhausted at this point, so we throw a RetryException with the
// last exception as the cause and remaining exceptions as suppressed exceptions.
RetryException retryException = new RetryException(
        "Retry policy for operation '%s' exhausted; aborting execution".formatted(retryableName),
        retryState);
this.retryListener.onRetryPolicyExhaustion(this.retryPolicy, retryable, retryException);
throw retryException;
```

`core/retry/RetryException.java`:

```java
RetryException(String message, RetryState retryState) {
    super(message, retryState.getLastException());
    List<Throwable> exceptions = retryState.getExceptions();
    for (int i = 0; i < exceptions.size() - 1; i++) { addSuppressed(exceptions.get(i)); }
}
@Override public final Throwable getCause() { return Objects.requireNonNull(super.getCause()); }
```

**Conclusion:** your caller catches **exactly the exception type thrown by the last attempt** — e.g. `HttpServerErrorException.ServiceUnavailable` or `ResourceAccessException`. `org.springframework.core.retry.RetryException` **never escapes** the `@Retryable` proxy. Consequence: the earlier attempts' exceptions, which were attached as *suppressed* on the discarded `RetryException`, are **lost** — the rethrown cause carries no suppressed siblings. If you want them, listen for `MethodRetryEvent` (section B).

Two other exhaustion paths take the same `catch (RetryException)` branch and are therefore also unwrapped: interruption during back-off, and `timeout()` expiry (`checkIfTimeoutExceeded` throws `RetryException`, whose cause is again the last recorded exception). So a `timeout` breach also surfaces as the last business exception, not as a `TimeoutException`.

Same-shape caveat for reactive return types: that path (`ReactorDelegate`) bypasses `RetryTemplate` entirely and uses `Mono/Flux.retryWhen`, so a reactive method **does** surface Reactor's `retryExhausted` exception. Not relevant if your method returns a plain value.

## A6. `includes` / `excludes` / `predicate` interaction

Two layers, both AND-ed, both on **assignability, traversing causes**.

Layer 1 — `AbstractRetryInterceptor.invoke` feeds all three into the policy separately:

```java
RetryPolicy retryPolicy = RetryPolicy.builder()
        .includes(spec.includes())
        .excludes(spec.excludes())
        .predicate(spec.predicate().forMethod(method))
        .maxRetries(spec.maxRetries())
        .timeout(spec.timeout())
        .delay(spec.delay()).jitter(spec.jitter())
        .multiplier(spec.multiplier()).maxDelay(spec.maxDelay())
        .build();
```

Layer 2 — `core/retry/DefaultRetryPolicy.shouldRetry`:

```java
@Override
public boolean shouldRetry(Throwable throwable) {
    return (this.exceptionFilter.match(throwable, true) &&
            (this.predicate == null || this.predicate.test(throwable)));
}
```

`exceptionFilter` is `new ExceptionTypeFilter(includes, excludes)` — the 2-arg ctor, whose Javadoc says "with the `matchIfEmpty` flag set to `true`". `match(throwable, true)` means **traverse causes**. `util/ExceptionTypeFilter.matchTraversingCauses`:

```java
boolean emptyIncludes = super.includes.isEmpty();
boolean emptyExcludes = super.excludes.isEmpty();
if (emptyIncludes && emptyExcludes) { return super.matchIfEmpty; }        // -> true
if (!emptyExcludes && matchTraversingCauses(exception, super.excludes)) { return false; }
return (emptyIncludes || matchTraversingCauses(exception, super.includes));
```
```java
for (Class<? extends Throwable> candidateType : candidateTypes) {
    Throwable current = exception;
    while (current != null) {
        if (match(current.getClass(), candidateType)) { return true; }
        current = current.getCause();
    }
}
```
```java
@Override protected boolean match(Class<? extends Throwable> instance, Class<? extends Throwable> candidate) {
    return candidate.isAssignableFrom(instance);       // assignability, not equality
}
```

Answers:
- **Only `includes` set** → retried iff the thrown exception **or any exception in its `getCause()` chain** is assignable to one of the listed types. Everything else is not retried and propagates on the first attempt.
- **`excludes` wins over `includes`** — the exclude check runs first and short-circuits to `false`.
- **Both empty** → retry on any `Throwable`.
- **`predicate` is AND-ed**, never OR-ed. Default `predicate()` is the marker `MethodRetryPredicate.class`, which `RetryAnnotationBeanPostProcessor.instantiatePredicate` turns into an always-true lambda:
  ```java
  if (predicateClass == MethodRetryPredicate.class) { return (method, throwable) -> true; }
  try { return (beanFactory != null ? beanFactory.createBean(predicateClass) : ...); }
  ```
  (so a custom predicate class **is created through the BeanFactory** and gets autowiring).
- `MethodRetrySpec.combinedPredicate()` composes the same AND for the reactive path:
  ```java
  MethodRetryPredicate combinedPredicate() {
      ExceptionTypeFilter exceptionFilter = new ExceptionTypeFilter(this.includes, this.excludes);
      return (method, throwable) -> exceptionFilter.match(throwable, true) &&
              this.predicate.shouldRetry(method, throwable);
  }
  ```

**Cause traversal is the tutorial-divergent bit**: `includes = HttpServerErrorException.class` will also retry a `SomeWrapper` whose cause is an `HttpServerErrorException`. Spring Retry's `retryFor` did not traverse causes.

## A7. Package-private class implementing a public interface — works, but read the two traps

Mechanics, all verified:

- `RetryAnnotationBeanPostProcessor extends AbstractBeanFactoryAwareAdvisingPostProcessor` → standard Spring AOP auto-proxying. Its pointcut is class-level **or** method-level:
  ```java
  Pointcut cpc = new AnnotationMatchingPointcut(Retryable.class, true);
  Pointcut mpc = new AnnotationMatchingPointcut(null, Retryable.class, true);
  this.advisor = new DefaultPointcutAdvisor(new ComposablePointcut(cpc).union(mpc), this.interceptor);
  ```
- `AbstractBeanFactoryAwareAdvisingPostProcessor.setBeanFactory` calls `AutoProxyUtils.applyDefaultProxyConfig(this, beanFactory)`, which copies from a `ProxyConfig` bean named `org.springframework.aop.framework.autoproxy.defaultProxyConfig` **for settings not locally set** (`ProxyConfig.copyDefault`: `if (this.proxyTargetClass == null) { this.proxyTargetClass = other.proxyTargetClass; }`).
- **In this project, that default is CGLIB.** `aspectjweaver-1.9.25.1.jar` is on your classpath, so Boot's `AopAutoConfiguration.AspectJAutoProxyingConfiguration.CglibAutoProxyConfiguration` applies (`@ConditionalOnBooleanProperty(name="spring.aop.proxy-target-class", matchIfMissing = true)` → `@EnableAspectJAutoProxy(proxyTargetClass = true)`), and `AspectJAutoProxyRegistrar` calls `AopConfigUtils.forceAutoProxyCreatorToUseClassProxying(registry)`, which is:
  ```java
  public static void forceAutoProxyCreatorToUseClassProxying(BeanDefinitionRegistry registry) {
      defaultProxyConfig(registry).getPropertyValues().add("proxyTargetClass", Boolean.TRUE);
  }
  ```
  → registers that `defaultProxyConfig` bean with `proxyTargetClass=true`.

**Trap 1 — `@EnableResilientMethods(proxyTargetClass = false)` does not force JDK proxies.** `ResilientMethodsConfiguration` only sets the flag when `true`; when `false` the field stays `null` and the CGLIB global default wins. To actually get a JDK proxy you need `spring.aop.proxy-target-class=false`, or the new Framework 7 `@org.springframework.context.annotation.Proxyable(ProxyType.INTERFACES)` on the bean class (verified present: `ctx/org/springframework/context/annotation/Proxyable.java`, `@since 7.0`, attributes `value()` / `interfaces()`).

**Trap 2 (only bites under a JDK proxy) — method-level `@Retryable` on an impl class is silently ignored.** Chain of verified facts:
- `JdkDynamicAopProxy` builds `new ReflectiveMethodInvocation(proxy, target, method, args, targetClass, chain)` where `method` is the **interface** method.
- `AbstractRetryInterceptor.invoke` does `Method method = invocation.getMethod(); ... getRetrySpec(method, target.getClass())`.
- `RetryAnnotationInterceptor.getRetrySpec` does `AnnotatedElementUtils.findMergedAnnotation(method, Retryable.class)`, and on `null` falls back to `findMergedAnnotation(targetClass, ...)` — **class level only**. It never calls `AopUtils.getMostSpecificMethod`.
- Meanwhile the *pointcut* does: `AnnotationMethodMatcher.matches` falls back to `AopUtils.getMostSpecificMethod(method, targetClass)`, so the advisor **is** applied.
- Net effect: proxy created, interceptor invoked, `spec == null`, `return invocation.proceed()` — **no retry, no error, no log**.
- Under CGLIB (your default) `invocation.getMethod()` is the target-class method, so this does not bite.

**Practical rules for a package-private impl of a public interface:**
- With the Boot default (CGLIB): fine. The class must be non-`final`, the annotated method non-`final`/non-`private`/non-`static`, and the class needs a non-private constructor. CGLIB generates the subclass in the same package, so package-private visibility is not itself a problem.
- If you switch to JDK proxies: put `@Retryable` on the **interface** method (or at class level), and inject the bean **by its interface type only** — the proxy is not castable to the package-private class.
- Either way, **self-invocation is not intercepted** (standard proxy semantics; the interceptor sits on the proxy).

# B. The retry event

## B8. FQCN and accessors

`org.springframework.resilience.retry.MethodRetryEvent` — note the package is `...resilience.**retry**`, **not** `...resilience.annotation`. `@since 7.0.3` (you are on 7.0.9, so it is present; it is absent in 7.0.0–7.0.2).

```
Compiled from "MethodRetryEvent.java"
public class org.springframework.resilience.retry.MethodRetryEvent extends org.springframework.context.event.MethodFailureEvent {
  private final boolean retryAborted;
  public org.springframework.resilience.retry.MethodRetryEvent(org.aopalliance.intercept.MethodInvocation, java.lang.Throwable, boolean);
  public java.lang.Throwable getFailure();
  public boolean isRetryAborted();
  public java.lang.String toString();
}
```

Superclass `org.springframework.context.event.MethodFailureEvent extends ApplicationEvent` (also `@since 7.0.3`):

```
public org.aopalliance.intercept.MethodInvocation getSource();
public java.lang.reflect.Method getMethod();
public java.lang.Throwable getFailure();
```

So a listener can read: **the `Method`**, **the `MethodInvocation`** (hence arguments, via `getSource().getArguments()`), **the `Throwable`**, **`isRetryAborted()`**, and `getTimestamp()` from `ApplicationEvent`. **There is no attempt/retry-count accessor** — you cannot read "attempt N" off the event. To recover the count on the terminal event, `getFailure()` is the `RetryException` and `((RetryException) e.getFailure()).getRetryCount()` works (`RetryException implements RetryState`, `getRetryCount() { return getSuppressed().length; }`).

Javadoc, verbatim:
> Event published for every exception encountered during retryable method invocation. Can be listened to via an `ApplicationListener<MethodRetryEvent>` bean or an `@EventListener(MethodRetryEvent.class)` method.

On `getFailure()`:
> This may be an exception thrown by the method or emitted by the reactive publisher returned from the method, **or a terminal exception on retry exhaustion, interruption or timeout**. For `RetryTemplate` executions, an `instanceof RetryException` check identifies a final exception.

On `isRetryAborted()`:
> If this returns `true`, `getFailure()` exposes **the final exception thrown by the retry infrastructure** (rather than thrown by the method itself).

## B9. Where it is published, and the gate

Two publication sites in `AbstractRetryInterceptor`, both routed through one private method:

Per-attempt (`retryAborted = false`), from the `RetryListener` the interceptor installs on its own `RetryTemplate`:

```java
retryTemplate.setRetryListener(new RetryListener() {
    @Override
    public void onRetryableExecution(RetryPolicy retryPolicy, Retryable<?> retryable, RetryState retryState) {
        if (!retryState.isSuccessful()) {
            onEvent(new MethodRetryEvent(invocation, retryState.getLastException(), false));
        }
    }
});
```

Terminal (`retryAborted = true`), in the exhaustion catch shown in A5: `onEvent(new MethodRetryEvent(invocation, ex, true));` where `ex` is the `RetryException` itself.

The gate:

```java
private void onEvent(MethodRetryEvent event) {
    logger.trace(event, event.getFailure());
    if (this.applicationEventPublisher != null) {
        this.applicationEventPublisher.publishEvent(event);
    }
}
```

**Gated only on an `ApplicationEventPublisher` having been injected — no property, no flag.** `AbstractRetryInterceptor implements ApplicationEventPublisherAware`, and `RetryAnnotationBeanPostProcessor` (itself `ApplicationEventPublisherAware`) forwards it:

```java
@Override public void setApplicationEventPublisher(ApplicationEventPublisher p) { this.interceptor.setApplicationEventPublisher(p); }
```

So inside a Spring context via `@EnableResilientMethods`, publication is effectively **unconditional**. It is `null` (silently no events) only if you construct `SimpleRetryInterceptor`/`AbstractRetryInterceptor` by hand outside the container. A `TRACE` log on `org.springframework.resilience.retry.AbstractRetryInterceptor` happens either way.

So for `maxRetries=3` and total failure you get **4** events: 3 with `retryAborted=false` (initial + retries 1,2 — precisely, one per failed execution) plus 1 with `retryAborted=true`. Exact count: one `false` event per failed attempt (initial attempt included), then one `true` event.

## B10. Non-event hook: yes — `org.springframework.core.retry.RetryListener` (spring-core)

```
public interface org.springframework.core.retry.RetryListener {
  public default void onRetryableExecution(RetryPolicy, Retryable<?>, RetryState);
  public default void beforeRetry(RetryPolicy, Retryable<?>, RetryState);
  public default void beforeRetry(RetryPolicy, Retryable<?>);
  public default void onRetrySuccess(RetryPolicy, Retryable<?>, java.lang.Object);
  public default void onRetryFailure(RetryPolicy, Retryable<?>, java.lang.Throwable);
  public default void onRetryPolicyExhaustion(RetryPolicy, Retryable<?>, RetryException);
  public default void onRetryPolicyInterruption(RetryPolicy, Retryable<?>, RetryException);
  public default void onRetryPolicyTimeout(RetryPolicy, Retryable<?>, RetryException);
}
```
Supporting types: `org.springframework.core.retry.RetryState` (`getRetryCount()`, `getExceptions()`, `getLastException()`, `isSuccessful()`) and `org.springframework.core.retry.support.CompositeRetryListener`.

**But it is not reachable from `@Retryable`.** `RetryTemplate.setRetryListener` takes a single listener, and `AbstractRetryInterceptor` **hard-codes its own anonymous listener** on the template it creates per invocation (code quoted in B9). `javap -p AbstractRetryInterceptor` shows **no** `setRetryListener` and no listener field. There is no `RetryListener` bean lookup anywhere in `org.springframework.resilience`.

**So: for annotation-driven retry, `MethodRetryEvent` is your only observability seam.** `RetryListener` only applies if you drive `RetryTemplate` yourself.

All except `withException` return `DefaultResponseCreator`, chainable with `.body(String)`, `.contentType(MediaType)`, `.header(String, String...)`, `.headers(HttpHeaders)`, `.location(URI)`, `.cookies(...)`.

`ResponseActions` is:
```java
ResponseActions andExpect(RequestMatcher requestMatcher);
void andRespond(ResponseCreator responseCreator);     // returns void -> one creator per expectation
```

**The exact script:**

```java
import static org.springframework.test.web.client.ExpectedCount.*;
import static org.springframework.test.web.client.match.MockRestRequestMatchers.*;
import static org.springframework.test.web.client.response.MockRestResponseCreators.*;

server.expect(times(2), requestTo("/rates/EUR"))
      .andExpect(method(HttpMethod.GET))
      .andRespond(withStatus(HttpStatus.SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE));   // or withServiceUnavailable()

server.expect(once(), requestTo("/rates/EUR"))
      .andExpect(method(HttpMethod.GET))
      .andRespond(withSuccess("{\"rate\":1.07}", MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON));

// ... call the retrying bean ...
server.verify();
```

**Why this yields 503, 503, 200 and not something else** — `SimpleRequestExpectationManager` (the default from `AbstractMockRestServiceServerBuilder.build()`) matches sequentially, with a repeat-group checked first:

```java
@Override
protected RequestExpectation matchRequest(ClientHttpRequest request) throws IOException {
    RequestExpectation expectation = this.repeatExpectations.findExpectation(request);
    if (expectation == null) {
        if (this.expectationIterator == null || !this.expectationIterator.hasNext()) {
            throw createUnexpectedRequestError(request);
        }
        expectation = this.expectationIterator.next();
        expectation.match(request);
    }
    this.repeatExpectations.update(expectation);
    return expectation;
}
```
and `RequestExpectationGroup.update`:
```java
public void update(RequestExpectation expectation) { expectation.incrementAndValidate(); updateInternal(expectation); }
private void updateInternal(RequestExpectation expectation) {
    if (expectation.hasRemainingCount()) { this.expectations.add(expectation); }
    else { this.expectations.remove(expectation); }
}
```
Request 1 → repeat group empty → iterator gives expectation #1 (count 2) → 503, remaining 1, stays in group. Request 2 → **found in repeat group** → 503, remaining 0, removed. Request 3 → group empty → iterator gives expectation #2 → 200. Class Javadoc, verbatim: *"When request expectations have an expected count greater than one, only the first execution is expected to match the order of declaration."*

Do **not** call `.ignoreExpectOrder(true)` here — that swaps in `UnorderedRequestExpectationManager` and your 503/200 ordering stops being guaranteed.

Between tests in the same class, call `server.reset()`.

**To script a timeout** instead of a status: `.andRespond(withException(new java.net.http.HttpTimeoutException("read timeout")))` — `withException(IOException)` is the only creator returning a bare `ResponseCreator`, and `HttpTimeoutException extends IOException`, so `RestClient` will wrap it into `ResourceAccessException` exactly as production would (see D17).

```
```java

    builder.requestFactory(this.requestFactoryBuilder.build(this.clientSettings));

**Per-client route works and is not clobbered**, for three verified reasons:

2. `configure(...)` runs **once, at bean creation**, before you get the instance. `DefaultRestClientBuilder.requestFactory` is a plain field write:
   ```java

## D17. Timeout exception — **`ResourceAccessException`, and its cause is NOT `SocketTimeoutException`**

`DefaultRestClient.DefaultRequestBodyUriSpec.exchangeInternal`:
```java
catch (IOException ex) {
    ResourceAccessException resourceAccessException = createResourceAccessException(uri, this.httpMethod, ex);
    if (observation != null) { observation.error(resourceAccessException); }
    throw resourceAccessException;
}
```
```java
private static ResourceAccessException createResourceAccessException(URI url, HttpMethod method, IOException ex) {
    StringBuilder msg = new StringBuilder("I/O error on ");
    ...
    return new ResourceAccessException(msg.toString(), ex);
}
```

`org.springframework.web.client.ResourceAccessException extends RestClientException` (→ `NestedRuntimeException` → unchecked).

**The cause, with the JDK factory this project gets:**
- **Read timeout** → `java.net.http.HttpTimeoutException`, thrown by `JdkClientHttpRequest.TimeoutHandler.handleCancellationException`:
  ```java
  public void handleCancellationException(CancellationException ex) throws HttpTimeoutException {
      if (this.timeout.get()) { throw new HttpTimeoutException(ex.getMessage()); }
  }
  ```
- **Connect timeout** → `java.net.http.HttpConnectTimeoutException` (a subclass of `HttpTimeoutException`, both `IOException`s) raised by the JDK client, surfaced through `JdkClientHttpRequest.executeInternal`'s `catch (ExecutionException ex)` → `else if (cause instanceof IOException ioEx) { throw ioEx; }`.

**Your catch must name `org.springframework.web.client.ResourceAccessException`.** `java.net.SocketTimeoutException` is what the *old* `SimpleClientHttpRequestFactory`/Apache path produced; on this classpath it will **never** appear. If you need to distinguish a timeout from other I/O failures, test `ex.getCause() instanceof java.net.http.HttpTimeoutException` — and note that `HttpConnectTimeoutException` is a subtype, so that one check covers both.

## D18. 503 vs 404 by default — both throw; 4xx and 5xx alike

Default handler is installed unconditionally in the `retrieve()` response spec's constructor (`DefaultRestClient.DefaultResponseSpec`):
```java
DefaultResponseSpec(RequestHeadersSpec<?> requestHeadersSpec) {
    this.requestHeadersSpec = requestHeadersSpec;
    this.statusHandlers.addAll(DefaultRestClient.this.defaultStatusHandlers);
    this.statusHandlers.add(StatusHandler.createDefaultStatusHandler(DefaultRestClient.this.messageConverters));
    this.defaultStatusHandlerCount = this.statusHandlers.size();
}
```
`StatusHandler.createDefaultStatusHandler`:
```java
public static StatusHandler createDefaultStatusHandler(List<HttpMessageConverter<?>> converters) {
    return new StatusHandler(response -> response.getStatusCode().isError(),
            (request, response) -> { throw createException(response, converters); });
}
```
`HttpStatusCode.isError()` is `is4xxClientError() || is5xxServerError()` → **yes, it throws for 4xx *and* 5xx**.
```java
if (statusCode.is4xxClientError()) {
    ex = HttpClientErrorException.create(message, statusCode, statusText, headers, body, charset);
}
else if (statusCode.is5xxServerError()) {
    ex = HttpServerErrorException.create(message, statusCode, statusText, headers, body, charset);
}
else {
    ex = new UnknownHttpStatusCodeException(message, statusCode.value(), statusText, headers, body, charset);
}
```

Verified hierarchy:
```
ResourceAccessException          extends RestClientException
RestClientResponseException      extends RestClientException
HttpClientErrorException         extends HttpStatusCodeException   (extends RestClientResponseException)
HttpServerErrorException         extends HttpStatusCodeException
HttpServerErrorException$ServiceUnavailable  extends HttpServerErrorException   (final)
HttpClientErrorException$NotFound            extends HttpClientErrorException   (final)
```

So on `retrieve().body(X)`:
- **503** → `HttpServerErrorException.ServiceUnavailable`
- **404** → `HttpClientErrorException.NotFound`
- any non-1xx/2xx/3xx code outside 4xx/5xx → `UnknownHttpStatusCodeException`
- both `.getStatusCode()`, `.getResponseBodyAsString()`, `.getResponseHeaders()` are available via `RestClientResponseException`.

Custom handlers registered via `onStatus(...)` are inserted **before** the defaults (`int index = this.statusHandlers.size() - this.defaultStatusHandlerCount; // Default handlers always last`), so `onStatus` reliably wins. The default handler applies to `retrieve()` only — `.exchange(...)` hands you the raw response with no status handling.

**Retry pairing:** to retry 5xx and connect/read failures but not 404, use
`@Retryable(includes = {HttpServerErrorException.class, ResourceAccessException.class}, maxRetries = 2, delay = 200, multiplier = 2.0, jitter = 50)`
— and remember A6's cause traversal, plus A5: after exhaustion your caller catches the `HttpServerErrorException.ServiceUnavailable` / `ResourceAccessException` directly.

# A. `@Retryable` / `@EnableResilientMethods`

## A1. FQCN — confirmed

`org.springframework.resilience.annotation.Retryable`, shipped in **spring-context** (`spring-context-7.0.9.jar`, entry `org/springframework/resilience/annotation/Retryable.class`). Declared `@Target({TYPE, METHOD}) @Retention(RUNTIME) @Documented @Reflective`, `@since 7.0`.

> ⚠️ **Import trap:** `org.springframework.core.retry.Retryable` also exists in spring-core and is **not** an annotation — it is the functional interface `Retryable<R>` that `RetryTemplate.execute(...)` takes. Both are on your classpath. `AbstractRetryInterceptor.java` imports the *core* one.

## A2. Every attribute, with types and defaults

`javap -p -classpath spring-context-7.0.9.jar org.springframework.resilience.annotation.Retryable`:

  public abstract java.lang.Class<? extends java.lang.Throwable>[] excludes();
  public abstract java.lang.Class<? extends org.springframework.resilience.retry.MethodRetryPredicate> predicate();

  public abstract java.lang.String maxRetriesString();
  public abstract long timeout();
  public abstract java.lang.String timeoutString();
  public abstract long delay();
  public abstract java.lang.String delayString();
  public abstract long jitter();
  public abstract java.lang.String jitterString();

  public abstract java.lang.String multiplierString();

There is no `retryFor`/`noRetryFor`/`label`/`stateful`/`listeners`/`recover`/`interceptor` attribute.

## A3. `@EnableResilientMethods`

`org.springframework.resilience.annotation.EnableResilientMethods` (spring-context). `@Target(TYPE) @Retention(RUNTIME) @Import(ResilientMethodsConfiguration.class)`.

```
public interface org.springframework.resilience.annotation.EnableResilientMethods extends java.lang.annotation.Annotation {
  public abstract boolean proxyTargetClass();   // default false
  public abstract int order();                  // default Ordered.LOWEST_PRECEDENCE - 1
}
```

**There is no `mode` attribute** (no AspectJ mode). Javadoc: "Enables Spring's core resilience features for method invocations: `@Retryable` as well as `@ConcurrencyLimit`." It imports `ResilientMethodsConfiguration`, which registers exactly two infrastructure beans:

```java
@Bean(name = "org.springframework.resilience.annotation.internalRetryAnnotationProcessor")
public RetryAnnotationBeanPostProcessor retryAdvisor() { ... }
@Bean(name = "org.springframework.resilience.annotation.internalConcurrencyLimitProcessor")
public ConcurrencyLimitBeanPostProcessor concurrencyLimitAdvisor() { ... }
```

**Boot 4.1.1 does NOT auto-configure this.** Verified: `spring-boot-autoconfigure-4.1.1.jar` contains no class matching `retry|resilien`, and its `AutoConfiguration.imports` has no matching entry. You must put `@EnableResilientMethods` on a `@Configuration` class yourself.

Note also `configureProxySupport` only ever calls `setProxyTargetClass(true)` when the attribute is `true` — it never calls `setProxyTargetClass(false)`. See A7 for why that matters.

## A4. `@Recover` equivalent — **NO. There is none.**

Verified negatively two ways: `unzip -l` over `spring-context-7.0.9.jar` and `spring-core-7.0.9.jar` filtered by `-i recover` returns **zero entries**; `grep -r "Recover"` across the extracted `org/springframework/resilience/**` and `org/springframework/core/retry/**` sources returns nothing. The complete `org.springframework.resilience` package is:

```
InvocationRejectedException
annotation/{ConcurrencyLimit, ConcurrencyLimitBeanPostProcessor, EnableResilientMethods,
            ResilientMethodsConfiguration, RetryAnnotationBeanPostProcessor, Retryable}
retry/{AbstractRetryInterceptor, MethodRetryEvent, MethodRetryPredicate,
       MethodRetrySpec, SimpleRetryInterceptor}
```

Fallback is your own `try/catch` around the proxied call.

## A5. **CRITICAL — what the caller sees on exhaustion: the last thrown exception, rethrown as-is.**

`org/springframework/resilience/retry/AbstractRetryInterceptor.java`, `invoke(...)`, lines 132–151 (verbatim):

```java
try {
    return retryTemplate.execute(new Retryable<@Nullable Object>() {
        @Override
        public @Nullable Object execute() throws Throwable {
            return (invocation instanceof ProxyMethodInvocation pmi ?
                    pmi.invocableClone().proceed() : invocation.proceed());
        }
        @Override
        public String getName() { return methodName; }
    });
}
catch (RetryException ex) {
    onEvent(new MethodRetryEvent(invocation, ex, true));
    if (logger.isDebugEnabled()) {
        logger.debug("Retryable operation '%s' failed".formatted(methodName), ex);
    }
    throw ex.getCause();          // <<<<<< unwrapped
}
```

And `RetryException`'s cause is definitionally the last exception — `core/retry/RetryTemplate.java` lines 194–200:

```java
// The RetryPolicy has exhausted at this point, so we throw a RetryException with the
// last exception as the cause and remaining exceptions as suppressed exceptions.
RetryException retryException = new RetryException(
        "Retry policy for operation '%s' exhausted; aborting execution".formatted(retryableName),
        retryState);
this.retryListener.onRetryPolicyExhaustion(this.retryPolicy, retryable, retryException);
throw retryException;
```

`core/retry/RetryException.java`:

```java
RetryException(String message, RetryState retryState) {
    super(message, retryState.getLastException());
    List<Throwable> exceptions = retryState.getExceptions();
    for (int i = 0; i < exceptions.size() - 1; i++) { addSuppressed(exceptions.get(i)); }
}
@Override public final Throwable getCause() { return Objects.requireNonNull(super.getCause()); }
```

**Conclusion:** your caller catches **exactly the exception type thrown by the last attempt** — e.g. `HttpServerErrorException.ServiceUnavailable` or `ResourceAccessException`. `org.springframework.core.retry.RetryException` **never escapes** the `@Retryable` proxy. Consequence: the earlier attempts' exceptions, which were attached as *suppressed* on the discarded `RetryException`, are **lost** — the rethrown cause carries no suppressed siblings. If you want them, listen for `MethodRetryEvent` (section B).

Two other exhaustion paths take the same `catch (RetryException)` branch and are therefore also unwrapped: interruption during back-off, and `timeout()` expiry (`checkIfTimeoutExceeded` throws `RetryException`, whose cause is again the last recorded exception). So a `timeout` breach also surfaces as the last business exception, not as a `TimeoutException`.

Same-shape caveat for reactive return types: that path (`ReactorDelegate`) bypasses `RetryTemplate` entirely and uses `Mono/Flux.retryWhen`, so a reactive method **does** surface Reactor's `retryExhausted` exception. Not relevant if your method returns a plain value.

## A6. `includes` / `excludes` / `predicate` interaction

Two layers, both AND-ed, both on **assignability, traversing causes**.

Layer 1 — `AbstractRetryInterceptor.invoke` feeds all three into the policy separately:

```java
RetryPolicy retryPolicy = RetryPolicy.builder()
        .includes(spec.includes())
        .excludes(spec.excludes())
        .predicate(spec.predicate().forMethod(method))
        .maxRetries(spec.maxRetries())
        .timeout(spec.timeout())
        .delay(spec.delay()).jitter(spec.jitter())
        .multiplier(spec.multiplier()).maxDelay(spec.maxDelay())
        .build();
```

Layer 2 — `core/retry/DefaultRetryPolicy.shouldRetry`:

```java
@Override
public boolean shouldRetry(Throwable throwable) {
    return (this.exceptionFilter.match(throwable, true) &&
            (this.predicate == null || this.predicate.test(throwable)));
}
```

`exceptionFilter` is `new ExceptionTypeFilter(includes, excludes)` — the 2-arg ctor, whose Javadoc says "with the `matchIfEmpty` flag set to `true`". `match(throwable, true)` means **traverse causes**. `util/ExceptionTypeFilter.matchTraversingCauses`:

```java
boolean emptyIncludes = super.includes.isEmpty();
boolean emptyExcludes = super.excludes.isEmpty();
if (emptyIncludes && emptyExcludes) { return super.matchIfEmpty; }        // -> true
if (!emptyExcludes && matchTraversingCauses(exception, super.excludes)) { return false; }
return (emptyIncludes || matchTraversingCauses(exception, super.includes));
```
```java
for (Class<? extends Throwable> candidateType : candidateTypes) {
    Throwable current = exception;
    while (current != null) {
        if (match(current.getClass(), candidateType)) { return true; }
        current = current.getCause();
    }
}
```
```java
@Override protected boolean match(Class<? extends Throwable> instance, Class<? extends Throwable> candidate) {
    return candidate.isAssignableFrom(instance);       // assignability, not equality
}
```

Answers:
- **Only `includes` set** → retried iff the thrown exception **or any exception in its `getCause()` chain** is assignable to one of the listed types. Everything else is not retried and propagates on the first attempt.
- **`excludes` wins over `includes`** — the exclude check runs first and short-circuits to `false`.
- **Both empty** → retry on any `Throwable`.
- **`predicate` is AND-ed**, never OR-ed. Default `predicate()` is the marker `MethodRetryPredicate.class`, which `RetryAnnotationBeanPostProcessor.instantiatePredicate` turns into an always-true lambda:
  ```java
  if (predicateClass == MethodRetryPredicate.class) { return (method, throwable) -> true; }
  try { return (beanFactory != null ? beanFactory.createBean(predicateClass) : ...); }
  ```
  (so a custom predicate class **is created through the BeanFactory** and gets autowiring).
- `MethodRetrySpec.combinedPredicate()` composes the same AND for the reactive path:
  ```java
  MethodRetryPredicate combinedPredicate() {
      ExceptionTypeFilter exceptionFilter = new ExceptionTypeFilter(this.includes, this.excludes);
      return (method, throwable) -> exceptionFilter.match(throwable, true) &&
              this.predicate.shouldRetry(method, throwable);
  }
  ```

**Cause traversal is the tutorial-divergent bit**: `includes = HttpServerErrorException.class` will also retry a `SomeWrapper` whose cause is an `HttpServerErrorException`. Spring Retry's `retryFor` did not traverse causes.

## A7. Package-private class implementing a public interface — works, but read the two traps

Mechanics, all verified:

- `RetryAnnotationBeanPostProcessor extends AbstractBeanFactoryAwareAdvisingPostProcessor` → standard Spring AOP auto-proxying. Its pointcut is class-level **or** method-level:
  ```java
  Pointcut cpc = new AnnotationMatchingPointcut(Retryable.class, true);
  Pointcut mpc = new AnnotationMatchingPointcut(null, Retryable.class, true);
  this.advisor = new DefaultPointcutAdvisor(new ComposablePointcut(cpc).union(mpc), this.interceptor);
  ```
- `AbstractBeanFactoryAwareAdvisingPostProcessor.setBeanFactory` calls `AutoProxyUtils.applyDefaultProxyConfig(this, beanFactory)`, which copies from a `ProxyConfig` bean named `org.springframework.aop.framework.autoproxy.defaultProxyConfig` **for settings not locally set** (`ProxyConfig.copyDefault`: `if (this.proxyTargetClass == null) { this.proxyTargetClass = other.proxyTargetClass; }`).
- **In this project, that default is CGLIB.** `aspectjweaver-1.9.25.1.jar` is on your classpath, so Boot's `AopAutoConfiguration.AspectJAutoProxyingConfiguration.CglibAutoProxyConfiguration` applies (`@ConditionalOnBooleanProperty(name="spring.aop.proxy-target-class", matchIfMissing = true)` → `@EnableAspectJAutoProxy(proxyTargetClass = true)`), and `AspectJAutoProxyRegistrar` calls `AopConfigUtils.forceAutoProxyCreatorToUseClassProxying(registry)`, which is:
  ```java
  public static void forceAutoProxyCreatorToUseClassProxying(BeanDefinitionRegistry registry) {
      defaultProxyConfig(registry).getPropertyValues().add("proxyTargetClass", Boolean.TRUE);
  }
  ```
  → registers that `defaultProxyConfig` bean with `proxyTargetClass=true`.

**Trap 1 — `@EnableResilientMethods(proxyTargetClass = false)` does not force JDK proxies.** `ResilientMethodsConfiguration` only sets the flag when `true`; when `false` the field stays `null` and the CGLIB global default wins. To actually get a JDK proxy you need `spring.aop.proxy-target-class=false`, or the new Framework 7 `@org.springframework.context.annotation.Proxyable(ProxyType.INTERFACES)` on the bean class (verified present: `ctx/org/springframework/context/annotation/Proxyable.java`, `@since 7.0`, attributes `value()` / `interfaces()`).

**Trap 2 (only bites under a JDK proxy) — method-level `@Retryable` on an impl class is silently ignored.** Chain of verified facts:
- `JdkDynamicAopProxy` builds `new ReflectiveMethodInvocation(proxy, target, method, args, targetClass, chain)` where `method` is the **interface** method.
- `AbstractRetryInterceptor.invoke` does `Method method = invocation.getMethod(); ... getRetrySpec(method, target.getClass())`.
- `RetryAnnotationInterceptor.getRetrySpec` does `AnnotatedElementUtils.findMergedAnnotation(method, Retryable.class)`, and on `null` falls back to `findMergedAnnotation(targetClass, ...)` — **class level only**. It never calls `AopUtils.getMostSpecificMethod`.
- Meanwhile the *pointcut* does: `AnnotationMethodMatcher.matches` falls back to `AopUtils.getMostSpecificMethod(method, targetClass)`, so the advisor **is** applied.
- Net effect: proxy created, interceptor invoked, `spec == null`, `return invocation.proceed()` — **no retry, no error, no log**.
- Under CGLIB (your default) `invocation.getMethod()` is the target-class method, so this does not bite.

**Practical rules for a package-private impl of a public interface:**
- With the Boot default (CGLIB): fine. The class must be non-`final`, the annotated method non-`final`/non-`private`/non-`static`, and the class needs a non-private constructor. CGLIB generates the subclass in the same package, so package-private visibility is not itself a problem.
- If you switch to JDK proxies: put `@Retryable` on the **interface** method (or at class level), and inject the bean **by its interface type only** — the proxy is not castable to the package-private class.
- Either way, **self-invocation is not intercepted** (standard proxy semantics; the interceptor sits on the proxy).

# B. The retry event

## B8. FQCN and accessors

`org.springframework.resilience.retry.MethodRetryEvent` — note the package is `...resilience.**retry**`, **not** `...resilience.annotation`. `@since 7.0.3` (you are on 7.0.9, so it is present; it is absent in 7.0.0–7.0.2).

```
Compiled from "MethodRetryEvent.java"
public class org.springframework.resilience.retry.MethodRetryEvent extends org.springframework.context.event.MethodFailureEvent {
  private final boolean retryAborted;
  public org.springframework.resilience.retry.MethodRetryEvent(org.aopalliance.intercept.MethodInvocation, java.lang.Throwable, boolean);
  public java.lang.Throwable getFailure();
  public boolean isRetryAborted();
  public java.lang.String toString();
}
```

Superclass `org.springframework.context.event.MethodFailureEvent extends ApplicationEvent` (also `@since 7.0.3`):

```
public org.aopalliance.intercept.MethodInvocation getSource();
public java.lang.reflect.Method getMethod();
public java.lang.Throwable getFailure();
```

So a listener can read: **the `Method`**, **the `MethodInvocation`** (hence arguments, via `getSource().getArguments()`), **the `Throwable`**, **`isRetryAborted()`**, and `getTimestamp()` from `ApplicationEvent`. **There is no attempt/retry-count accessor** — you cannot read "attempt N" off the event. To recover the count on the terminal event, `getFailure()` is the `RetryException` and `((RetryException) e.getFailure()).getRetryCount()` works (`RetryException implements RetryState`, `getRetryCount() { return getSuppressed().length; }`).

Javadoc, verbatim:
> Event published for every exception encountered during retryable method invocation. Can be listened to via an `ApplicationListener<MethodRetryEvent>` bean or an `@EventListener(MethodRetryEvent.class)` method.

On `getFailure()`:
> This may be an exception thrown by the method or emitted by the reactive publisher returned from the method, **or a terminal exception on retry exhaustion, interruption or timeout**. For `RetryTemplate` executions, an `instanceof RetryException` check identifies a final exception.

On `isRetryAborted()`:
> If this returns `true`, `getFailure()` exposes **the final exception thrown by the retry infrastructure** (rather than thrown by the method itself).

## B9. Where it is published, and the gate

Two publication sites in `AbstractRetryInterceptor`, both routed through one private method:

Per-attempt (`retryAborted = false`), from the `RetryListener` the interceptor installs on its own `RetryTemplate`:

```java
retryTemplate.setRetryListener(new RetryListener() {
    @Override
    public void onRetryableExecution(RetryPolicy retryPolicy, Retryable<?> retryable, RetryState retryState) {
        if (!retryState.isSuccessful()) {
            onEvent(new MethodRetryEvent(invocation, retryState.getLastException(), false));
        }
    }
});
```

Terminal (`retryAborted = true`), in the exhaustion catch shown in A5: `onEvent(new MethodRetryEvent(invocation, ex, true));` where `ex` is the `RetryException` itself.

The gate:

```java
private void onEvent(MethodRetryEvent event) {
    logger.trace(event, event.getFailure());
    if (this.applicationEventPublisher != null) {
        this.applicationEventPublisher.publishEvent(event);
    }
}
```

**Gated only on an `ApplicationEventPublisher` having been injected — no property, no flag.** `AbstractRetryInterceptor implements ApplicationEventPublisherAware`, and `RetryAnnotationBeanPostProcessor` (itself `ApplicationEventPublisherAware`) forwards it:

```java
@Override public void setApplicationEventPublisher(ApplicationEventPublisher p) { this.interceptor.setApplicationEventPublisher(p); }
```

So inside a Spring context via `@EnableResilientMethods`, publication is effectively **unconditional**. It is `null` (silently no events) only if you construct `SimpleRetryInterceptor`/`AbstractRetryInterceptor` by hand outside the container. A `TRACE` log on `org.springframework.resilience.retry.AbstractRetryInterceptor` happens either way.

So for `maxRetries=3` and total failure you get **4** events: 3 with `retryAborted=false` (initial + retries 1,2 — precisely, one per failed execution) plus 1 with `retryAborted=true`. Exact count: one `false` event per failed attempt (initial attempt included), then one `true` event.

## B10. Non-event hook: yes — `org.springframework.core.retry.RetryListener` (spring-core)

```
public interface org.springframework.core.retry.RetryListener {
  public default void onRetryableExecution(RetryPolicy, Retryable<?>, RetryState);
  public default void beforeRetry(RetryPolicy, Retryable<?>, RetryState);
  public default void beforeRetry(RetryPolicy, Retryable<?>);
  public default void onRetrySuccess(RetryPolicy, Retryable<?>, java.lang.Object);
  public default void onRetryFailure(RetryPolicy, Retryable<?>, java.lang.Throwable);
  public default void onRetryPolicyExhaustion(RetryPolicy, Retryable<?>, RetryException);
  public default void onRetryPolicyInterruption(RetryPolicy, Retryable<?>, RetryException);
  public default void onRetryPolicyTimeout(RetryPolicy, Retryable<?>, RetryException);
}
```
Supporting types: `org.springframework.core.retry.RetryState` (`getRetryCount()`, `getExceptions()`, `getLastException()`, `isSuccessful()`) and `org.springframework.core.retry.support.CompositeRetryListener`.

**But it is not reachable from `@Retryable`.** `RetryTemplate.setRetryListener` takes a single listener, and `AbstractRetryInterceptor` **hard-codes its own anonymous listener** on the template it creates per invocation (code quoted in B9). `javap -p AbstractRetryInterceptor` shows **no** `setRetryListener` and no listener field. There is no `RetryListener` bean lookup anywhere in `org.springframework.resilience`.

**So: for annotation-driven retry, `MethodRetryEvent` is your only observability seam.** `RetryListener` only applies if you drive `RetryTemplate` yourself.

**The exact script:**

import static org.springframework.test.web.client.match.MockRestRequestMatchers.*;
import static org.springframework.test.web.client.response.MockRestResponseCreators.*;

server.expect(times(2), requestTo("/rates/EUR"))

server.expect(once(), requestTo("/rates/EUR"))

// ... call the retrying bean ...
server.verify();
```

**Why this yields 503, 503, 200 and not something else** — `SimpleRequestExpectationManager` (the default from `AbstractMockRestServiceServerBuilder.build()`) matches sequentially, with a repeat-group checked first:

```java
@Override
protected RequestExpectation matchRequest(ClientHttpRequest request) throws IOException {
    RequestExpectation expectation = this.repeatExpectations.findExpectation(request);
    if (expectation == null) {
        if (this.expectationIterator == null || !this.expectationIterator.hasNext()) {
            throw createUnexpectedRequestError(request);
        }
        expectation = this.expectationIterator.next();
        expectation.match(request);
    }
    this.repeatExpectations.update(expectation);
    return expectation;
}
```
and `RequestExpectationGroup.update`:
```java
public void update(RequestExpectation expectation) { expectation.incrementAndValidate(); updateInternal(expectation); }
private void updateInternal(RequestExpectation expectation) {
    if (expectation.hasRemainingCount()) { this.expectations.add(expectation); }
    else { this.expectations.remove(expectation); }
}
```
Request 1 → repeat group empty → iterator gives expectation #1 (count 2) → 503, remaining 1, stays in group. Request 2 → **found in repeat group** → 503, remaining 0, removed. Request 3 → group empty → iterator gives expectation #2 → 200. Class Javadoc, verbatim: *"When request expectations have an expected count greater than one, only the first execution is expected to match the order of declaration."*

Do **not** call `.ignoreExpectOrder(true)` here — that swaps in `UnorderedRequestExpectationManager` and your 503/200 ordering stops being guaranteed.

Between tests in the same class, call `server.reset()`.

**To script a timeout** instead of a status: `.andRespond(withException(new java.net.http.HttpTimeoutException("read timeout")))` — `withException(IOException)` is the only creator returning a bare `ResponseCreator`, and `HttpTimeoutException extends IOException`, so `RestClient` will wrap it into `ResourceAccessException` exactly as production would (see D17).

```java

**Per-client route works and is not clobbered**, for three verified reasons:

1. The builder bean is **prototype-scoped** — class Javadoc: *"This will produce a `RestClient.Builder` bean with the `prototype` scope, meaning each injection point will receive a newly cloned instance of the builder."* Your mutation cannot leak to other clients.
2. `configure(...)` runs **once, at bean creation**, before you get the instance. `DefaultRestClientBuilder.requestFactory` is a plain field write:

## D17. Timeout exception — **`ResourceAccessException`, and its cause is NOT `SocketTimeoutException`**

`DefaultRestClient.DefaultRequestBodyUriSpec.exchangeInternal`:
```java
catch (IOException ex) {
    ResourceAccessException resourceAccessException = createResourceAccessException(uri, this.httpMethod, ex);
    if (observation != null) { observation.error(resourceAccessException); }
    throw resourceAccessException;
}
```
```java

    StringBuilder msg = new StringBuilder("I/O error on ");
    ...
    return new ResourceAccessException(msg.toString(), ex);
}
```

`org.springframework.web.client.ResourceAccessException extends RestClientException` (→ `NestedRuntimeException` → unchecked).

**The cause, with the JDK factory this project gets:**
- **Read timeout** → `java.net.http.HttpTimeoutException`, thrown by `JdkClientHttpRequest.TimeoutHandler.handleCancellationException`:
  ```java
  public void handleCancellationException(CancellationException ex) throws HttpTimeoutException {
      if (this.timeout.get()) { throw new HttpTimeoutException(ex.getMessage()); }
  }
  ```
- **Connect timeout** → `java.net.http.HttpConnectTimeoutException` (a subclass of `HttpTimeoutException`, both `IOException`s) raised by the JDK client, surfaced through `JdkClientHttpRequest.executeInternal`'s `catch (ExecutionException ex)` → `else if (cause instanceof IOException ioEx) { throw ioEx; }`.

**Your catch must name `org.springframework.web.client.ResourceAccessException`.** `java.net.SocketTimeoutException` is what the *old* `SimpleClientHttpRequestFactory`/Apache path produced; on this classpath it will **never** appear. If you need to distinguish a timeout from other I/O failures, test `ex.getCause() instanceof java.net.http.HttpTimeoutException` — and note that `HttpConnectTimeoutException` is a subtype, so that one check covers both.

## D18. 503 vs 404 by default — both throw; 4xx and 5xx alike

Default handler is installed unconditionally in the `retrieve()` response spec's constructor (`DefaultRestClient.DefaultResponseSpec`):
```java
DefaultResponseSpec(RequestHeadersSpec<?> requestHeadersSpec) {
    this.requestHeadersSpec = requestHeadersSpec;
    this.statusHandlers.addAll(DefaultRestClient.this.defaultStatusHandlers);
    this.statusHandlers.add(StatusHandler.createDefaultStatusHandler(DefaultRestClient.this.messageConverters));
    this.defaultStatusHandlerCount = this.statusHandlers.size();
}
```
`StatusHandler.createDefaultStatusHandler`:
```java
public static StatusHandler createDefaultStatusHandler(List<HttpMessageConverter<?>> converters) {
    return new StatusHandler(response -> response.getStatusCode().isError(),
            (request, response) -> { throw createException(response, converters); });
}
```
`HttpStatusCode.isError()` is `is4xxClientError() || is5xxServerError()` → **yes, it throws for 4xx *and* 5xx**.
```java
if (statusCode.is4xxClientError()) {
    ex = HttpClientErrorException.create(message, statusCode, statusText, headers, body, charset);
}
else if (statusCode.is5xxServerError()) {
    ex = HttpServerErrorException.create(message, statusCode, statusText, headers, body, charset);
}
else {
    ex = new UnknownHttpStatusCodeException(message, statusCode.value(), statusText, headers, body, charset);
}
```

Verified hierarchy:
```
ResourceAccessException          extends RestClientException
RestClientResponseException      extends RestClientException
HttpClientErrorException         extends HttpStatusCodeException   (extends RestClientResponseException)
HttpServerErrorException         extends HttpStatusCodeException
HttpServerErrorException$ServiceUnavailable  extends HttpServerErrorException   (final)
HttpClientErrorException$NotFound            extends HttpClientErrorException   (final)
```

So on `retrieve().body(X)`:
- **503** → `HttpServerErrorException.ServiceUnavailable`
- **404** → `HttpClientErrorException.NotFound`
- any non-1xx/2xx/3xx code outside 4xx/5xx → `UnknownHttpStatusCodeException`
- both `.getStatusCode()`, `.getResponseBodyAsString()`, `.getResponseHeaders()` are available via `RestClientResponseException`.

Custom handlers registered via `onStatus(...)` are inserted **before** the defaults (`int index = this.statusHandlers.size() - this.defaultStatusHandlerCount; // Default handlers always last`), so `onStatus` reliably wins. The default handler applies to `retrieve()` only — `.exchange(...)` hands you the raw response with no status handling.

**Retry pairing:** to retry 5xx and connect/read failures but not 404, use
`@Retryable(includes = {HttpServerErrorException.class, ResourceAccessException.class}, maxRetries = 2, delay = 200, multiplier = 2.0, jitter = 50)`
— and remember A6's cause traversal, plus A5: after exhaustion your caller catches the `HttpServerErrorException.ServiceUnavailable` / `ResourceAccessException` directly.

The **read** timeout type (`HttpTimeoutException`) is directly quoted from `TimeoutHandler`.

**Where the real API differs from a pre-Framework-7 / pre-Boot-4 tutorial:**
1. `@Retryable` is Framework core now (`org.springframework.resilience.annotation`), **not** `org.springframework.retry.annotation` — and **no `spring-retry` dependency, no `@EnableRetry`**. The enabler is `@EnableResilientMethods`, and **Boot does not auto-configure it**.
2. `maxRetries` (default 3), not `maxAttempts` (default 3 *attempts*). Same number, different meaning: Framework 7 does 1 + 3 = **4** total calls.
3. No `@Backoff` annotation; no `@Recover`; no `RetryTemplate` bean, no `RetryListener` bean pickup for annotated methods. Observability is `MethodRetryEvent` only.
4. `includes`/`excludes` **traverse the cause chain**; `retryFor`/`noRetryFor` did not.
5. `ClientHttpRequestFactorySettings` is **gone**; it is `HttpClientSettings`, and the package moved from `org.springframework.boot.web.client` to `org.springframework.boot.http.client`, into a **separate artifact** (`spring-boot-http-client`) that `spring-boot-starter-webmvc` does not pull.
6. `spring.http.client.connect-timeout` / `read-timeout` are **deprecated since 4.0.0** in favour of `spring.http.clients.*` (plural).
7. `@AutoConfigureMockRestServiceServer` moved to `org.springframework.boot.restclient.test.autoconfigure` in artifact `spring-boot-restclient-test` — **not** on this project's classpath.
8. The default `ClientHttpRequestFactory` in Boot 4 on a bare classpath is `JdkClientHttpRequestFactory`, **not** `SimpleClientHttpRequestFactory` — so a timeout's cause is `java.net.http.HttpTimeoutException`, **not** `java.net.SocketTimeoutException`.

# stand-in FX provider, which a bounded thread pool can deadlock on. See
# docs/design-decisions.md 27-28.

spring.jackson.deserialization.accept-float-as-int=false

spring.datasource.url=jdbc:h2:mem:payments;DB_CLOSE_DELAY=-1
spring.datasource.username=sa
spring.datasource.password=

# The H2 console is deliberately not enabled: the security chain denies /h2-console

# Flyway owns the schema; Hibernate only checks the entities against it and
# never emits DDL. See docs/design-decisions.md 29.
spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=validate

# The Vite dev server, which runs as its own process on a different origin. A

# The Exchange Rate provider's root. Points at this application's own stand-in, which

payments.fx.base-url=http://localhost:8080/mock

# A slow provider must not park a request holding an in-progress Idempotency Key, so
# both bounds are set. The read timeout is well above the stand-in's configurable
# latency, so raising that dial reaches the timeout path rather than a hung test.
payments.fx.connect-timeout=1s
payments.fx.read-timeout=2s

# Retries after the first attempt, so a failing provider is called three times. These
# two live here rather than as defaults on ExchangeRateSettings because @Retryable
# reads them as ${...} placeholders, which see the environment and not the record.
payments.fx.max-retries=2
payments.fx.retry-delay=100ms

## What was built

`ExchangeRateProvider` (public port, one method `ExchangeRate exchangeRateFor(Currency base, Currency quote)`); `ExchangeRate` (public record: base, quote, rate, fetchedAt); `ExchangeRateUnavailableException` (public); `ExchangeRateSettings` (`@ConfigurationProperties("payments.fx")`); `ExchangeRateConfiguration` (`@EnableResilientMethods`, the `RestClient` bean); `RetriedQuotes` (package-private, carries `@Retryable`); `ProviderQuote` (package-private wire record); `HttpExchangeRateProvider` (package-private, implements the port). 1. **The `ExchangeRate` type ticket 07 deferred was born here, and it is a weaker claim than it looks.** Ticket 07 parked it for "25 or 26, once there is something real to model". The provider quotes a pair and a number — no timestamp, no validity window. So `fetchedAt` is read from this application's injected `Clock` when the response arrives: it records when *we* learned the rate, not when the market set it. That is the only claim the wire supports, and §15 needs it stored on the Transfer, so ticket 26 stores the record whole.

2. **Spring Framework 7 has no `@Recover`, and on exhaustion rethrows the last attempt's exception unwrapped.** Verified in `AbstractRetryInterceptor.invoke`: it catches `RetryException` and does `throw ex.getCause()`. The `RetryException` — which carried the earlier attempts as *suppressed* exceptions and knew the retry count — never escapes the proxy. Consequence, and it is structural: nothing at the catch site can distinguish "the provider returned 503" from "the provider returned 503 three times", so the mapping of the provider's failures onto ours cannot live in the retried method. It sits in a second bean *above* it (`HttpExchangeRateProvider` over `RetriedQuotes`), because a call from a class to its own `@Retryable` method bypasses the proxy and would never retry at all. The two-class shape is forced by the framework, not chosen for tidiness.

3. **The attempt count in the exception is read from the policy, not observed.** Follows from (2): the object that knew the real count was discarded by the interceptor. `ExchangeRateUnavailableException` reports `maxRetries + 1` from the same setting the annotation counted with. A default on the record would be invisible to the annotation; a second one written inline in the placeholder is exactly the drift the single-copy rule exists to prevent. So `ExchangeRateSettings` binds with no fallbacks and the defaults sit in `application.properties`, where both readers look — a deliberate departure from the rule `FlakinessSettings` states, for a case that rule did not anticipate. A deployment that deletes a line now fails at startup instead of quietly retrying a different number of times than it documents.

5. **§28 named the property `fx.base-url`; every property in this application is under `payments.`.** It is `payments.fx.base-url`. This is a false sentence in §28 and should be corrected in place per AGENTS.md, with the correction recorded in the ticket file.

6. **Never retrying `4xx` is implemented by not naming it, and a refusal is a different failure from an outage.** `includes = {HttpServerErrorException.class, ResourceAccessException.class}`; anything else propagates from the first attempt. The echo is compared and a mismatch is an `IllegalStateException`, the same unchecked-because-it-is-a-bug-above-us reasoning as ticket 07's rate of zero.
